extractedPages.text: Glass Recycling to Foam-Glass Products – Detailed Business Plan Document version: v1.0 Date: 2026-04-08 Author: Tomas Svoboda Scope: Concept / pre-FEED business and technical pack Location: Curaçao

4 This document expands the initial concept note into a pre-FEED level business and technical plan. It is intentionally more conservative where real-world bottlenecks exist, especially around feedstock capture, usable waste heat, process water and island-specific execution risk. Why? • Solving trouble with glass waste on the ABC islands • Creating locally necessary material for building construction • Creating new jobs and support economy during factory building (preferred local suppliers) 1. Executive framing The project converts mixed waste glass from Curaçao (and ideal from Aruba and Bonaire too) into two core products: foam-glass aggregate and foam-glass blocks. The reference production concept is a 30 m electric tunnel kiln with annual output of about 19,162 m³/yr at 75% calendar utilization, equivalent to about 2,951 t/yr of finished product. The central strategic logic is import substitution and waste reduction. The plant does not need enormous tonnage to operate. In the base case it needs only about 3,451 t/yr of mixed raw glass at the factory gate. That is small enough to be plausible on Curaçao, but large enough that it still requires deliberate collection contracts rather than passive assumptions. Three corrections materially change the economics compared with an optimistic first-pass concept: • The kiln's recoverable low-grade heat should not be valued as if 150–250 kW can always be consumed. In the base case the realistic wash + dry thermal sink is only about 159 MWhth/yr on average, or roughly 73 kWth if the wash line runs one 8-hour shift. • Dedicated desalination is not justified for phase 1. Process make-up water is only about 248 m³/yr, so buying industrial water is cheaper and far simpler if a utility connection exists. • A battery should be justified primarily by resilience, power-quality support and operating flexibility, not by energy arbitrage. The current industrial high/low tariff spread is too small for a pure tariff-arbitrage case. Finances CAPEX is in basic version of plan 19,600,000 USD, but it can be optimi zed 17,600,000 USD by splitting some investments into next phases of project without af fecting start of the project. CAPEX must be considered over time (project contains building constructions, large technologies => spread over 1-2y). OPEX total revenue is modeled between 3,7-4,4mil.USD based on scenario. Main items on expenses side are: - Payroll: 1mil.USD (30 FTE) - Grid electricity: 0.48mil.USD - Maintenance: 0.25mil.USD - Collection and transport: 0.24mil.USD - Other: 0.6-0.8mil.USD Realistic pure possible payback of investment is between 12-15 years. It does not consider other efects on local economy, that cret es huge additional value such as decrease need for concrete, free up areas for storing glass waste, back investment to local economy during building factory, creating new jobs and other non-financial aspects. Project is not suitable for pure financial investor, but great profitable step for government.

5 2. What the plant will make and why it should exist The plant will manufacture two foam-glass product families from mixed bottle and flat-glass waste: • Foam-glass aggregate: 11,498 m³/yr in the base case. This is the lower-finishing, easier-to-place product. It is relevant for lightweight fill, drainage layers, sub-base, roof build-ups and insulating fill. • Foam-glass blocks / bricks: 7,665 m³/yr in the base case. This product commands a higher selling price but requires stricter process control, cutting, trimming and pallet handling. Foam-glass blocks/slabs Foam-glass aggregate / gravel A dual-product strategy is important on an island. Aggregate gives a broad local outlet and tolerates a slightly wider process window. Blocks create margin and visibility, but they should not be the only route to market. The recommended starting mix is 60% aggregate and 40% blocks by volume, with the option to flex after market testing. The plant should not be treated as a generic recycling line. It is a specialty thermal-processing plant that happens to use waste glass as feedstock. That means the real value drivers are recipe stability, thermal control, capture logistics, and local market realization rather than the mere fact that a kiln exists.
6 Figure 1. Detailed process flow used for the base concept.

7 3. Demand and market logic The local business case depends on replacing imported lightweight fill and insulation materials whose delivered island cost is elevated by freight, handling and inventory. That is why the plan deliberately uses local selling-price ranges rather than mainland commodity assumptions. In the base scenario the model uses 165 USD/m³ for aggregate and 240 USD/m³ for blocks. These are not 'guaranteed' market prices, with actual geopolitical situation you can expect large inflation in next years. Same as price of the sand usable in concrete, that increase demand for fillings that can be used in concrete (for example glass foam). They are planning values that still need confirmation by contractor interviews, pilot samples and delivered-import benchmarking. The right commercial posture is not 'cheap recycled material'. It is 'local engineered lightweight insulation / fill with lower logistics friction, shorter lead time and visible environmental value'. The nearer the project gets to construction and hospitality buyers, the more defensible the product premium becomes. • Anchor customers should include civil contractors, roofing and waterproofing contractors, resort and hotel owners, developers, and public infrastructure programs. • At least 70% of base output should be covered by anchor offtake before final investment approval. The plant should not rely on discovering the market after commissioning. • Export to nearby islands can be opportunistic, but the base project should stand on Curaçao demand plus only modest export flexibility. Figure 2. EBITDA sensitivity across conservative, base and upside operating envelopes.

8 4. Feedstock strategy and can the island really support the plant? The plant's base mixed-glass requirement is about 3,451 t/yr. This is the single most important physical constraint because the kiln prefers continuous operation and because feedstock shortfall is much harder to fix later than payroll or packaging cost. There is no reliable single official number in the project pack that proves, by itself, that Curaçao already delivers this exact quantity of clean and capturable mixed glass. Therefore the project should be framed honestly: feedstock sufficiency must be demonstrated by a capture model plus signed contracts, not by wishful top-down waste percentages. The most practical approach is a bottom-up capture model built from four streams: • Residents and retail drop-off. • Stayover tourism / HORECA (hotels, bars, restaurants, resorts). • Construction and demolition flat glass from windows and renovation. • Optional neighboring-island top-up only as a buffer, not the primary business case. Table 1. Modeled capturable mixed-glass envelope (planning assumption, not official waste statistics). Segment Driver Low t/yr Base t/yr High t/yr Residents & retail 160,000 residents 960.00 1,600.00 2,240.00 Stayover tourism / HORECA 788,427 stayover visitors x 8.4 nights 993.42 1,457.01 1,854.38 Cruise day visitors 881,665 cruise visitors 17.63 35.27 52.90 Construction & demolition flat glass Window replacement / demolition 250.00 500.00 800.00 Neighbor island top-up (optional) Aruba/Bonaire if needed 0.00 0.00 1,000.00 Total modeled capturable mixed glass 2,221.05 3,592.28 5,947.28 The modeled base capture case reaches about 3,592 t/yr, which is only modestly above the base plant need of 3,451 t/yr. That is simultaneously encouraging and a warning. It means the plant is not absurdly oversized for the island, but it also means execution has to be disciplined. A weak collection program could easily underfeed the plant. Those numbers are just for Curaçao. It would be good to consider collection of glass from Aruba and Bonaire too. If all islands will participate, it would be possible to increase the capacity of the plant, that can lead to better EBIDTA. A sensible pre-FID target is therefore at least 4.0–4.2 kt/yr of contracted mixed-glass supply, leaving some margin above modeled base need. That contract basket should combine municipal / partner collection, hotel and resort contracts, and construction-window recovery. A separate sense-check also helps. Beer imports alone are large enough to indicate that beverage packaging flow is meaningful on the island, even though not all of that volume is in recoverable glass

9 bottles. The purpose of that benchmark is not to prove the exact answer, but to confirm that the plant's 3.45 kt/yr requirement is not outlandish in scale. Figure 3. Modeled base feedstock segments compared with raw-glass need.

10 5. Collection and transport logistics Collection design matters more than people often expect. Because the plant's annual feedstock need is moderate rather than massive, it is usually smarter to optimize routing, consolidation and contamination control than to overinvest in a large owned fleet on day one. Table 2. Base-case logistics quantities. Metric Value Unit Comment Plant raw glass need 3,451.27 t/yr Mixed bottles, jars and flat glass into factory gate Direct collection routes 986.08 loaded trips/yr If 3.5 t route trucks drive directly to plant Factory line-haul inbound 493.04 loaded trips/yr If glass is consolidated into 7 t bulk deliveries to plant Outbound product deliveries 547.50 loaded trips/yr At 35 m3 average shipment Block pallets 6,387.50 pallets/yr Assuming 1.2 m3 palletized block shipment Aggregate big-bags 7,665.00 big-bags/yr Assuming 1.5 m3 per big-bag Sea top-up equivalent 172.56 20 t containers/yr Only if all feedstock came by sea from neighboring islands The practical implication is straightforward. If all hotel / bar material were delivered directly to the plant by small route trucks, the model implies roughly 986 loaded trips per year, or a little over three loaded routes per collection day. If glass is first consolidated into a central transfer point and then line-hauled to the plant in 7 t loads, that falls to roughly 493 loaded factory-inbound trips per year. For that reason, the reference design assumes the core plant is built without a full islandwide self-owned collection fleet. Instead, collection is handled by partner routes, a municipal interface, outsourced transport, or a later optional fleet add-on. The factory's core economics should not be burdened with a fully in-house route network before the feedstock basin is proven. Sea logistics should remain optional. The former refinery setting makes marine access attractive, but the base business case should not rely on inter-island shipping. Marine top-up is best used as contingency capacity after local collection is functioning.
11 Figure 4. Concept site masterplan on a former refinery parcel.

12 6. Process and technology basis The chosen flow sheet is intentionally conventional rather than exotic. That improves serviceability and de- risks spare parts on an island: • Receiving, stockpiling and pre-sort. • Mechanical separation: trommel / screens, ferrous and non-ferrous metal removal, optical sorting. • Wash, rinse, dryer and recirculating water loop with filter-press sludge handling. • Coarse crushing and fine milling to glass flour. • Silos, gravimetric dosing and intensive mixing with a foaming package and process aids. • Forming and continuous passage through a 30 m electric tunnel kiln. • Controlled cooling and split into two finishing streams: block trimming / palletizing and aggregate crushing / bagging. The recipe is still a pilot-trial matter, not a fixed procurement list. For concept modeling, it is enough to assume that purchased additives equal about 2.5% of clean-glass mass. That package can include the foaming agent itself plus one or more process aids. The plant should not commit to a final additive package until real Curaçao cullet blends are tested, especially because flat-glass fractions can shift viscosity and foaming behavior. The base material balance indicates 2,968 t/yr of clean glass plus 74 t/yr of additives to produce 2,951 t/yr of finished foam-glass products. Table 3. Base material balance. Metric Base value Unit Annual product output 19,162.50 m3/yr Aggregate output 11,497.50 m3/yr Block output 7,665.00 m3/yr Product mass 2,951.03 t/yr Clean glass required 2,968.09 t/yr Additives purchased 74.20 t/yr Raw mixed glass required 3,451.27 t/yr Rejects removed 483.18 t/yr Average density 154.00 kg/m3 The tunnel kiln is modeled as a 1 MW connected load with a lower average operating draw in steady production. This distinction matters. If the kiln truly averaged 1 MW continuously all year, the specific energy intensity would be too high relative to benchmark foam-glass processes. The planning model therefore treats 1 MW as installed/available capacity and about 550 kW as a realistic base running draw during stable production.
13 Figure 5. Internal hall arrangement showing the planned west-to-east material flow.

14 7. Energy model and why the 'waste heat' story must stay realistic Total base-case plant electricity is modeled at about 4,052 MWh/yr or 211.4 kWh/m³. Of that, the kiln itself is about 3,614 MWh/yr and auxiliaries about 438 MWh/yr. Table 4. Base-case electricity load breakdown. Load block MWh/yr Share % Electric tunnel kiln incl. soak/cooling fans 3,613.50 89.19 Sorting, screens, magnets, optical sorter 70.00 1.73 Wash pumps, recirculation and filter press 55.00 1.36 Dryer fans / exhaust handling 45.00 1.11 Coarse crushing 35.00 0.86 Fine milling and classification 95.00 2.34 Mixing, dosing, forming and product handling 48.00 1.18 Dust collection, compressed air, lighting, controls, misc. 90.09 2.22 Own renewable generation from 1 MWp PV and 200 kW wind is modeled at about 2,496 MWh/yr, of which roughly 2,296 MWh/yr is self-consumed on site. Grid import remains material at about 1,756 MWh/yr, which is why grid quality and backup strategy still matter. The essential insight is that heat recovery must be matched to a real thermal sink. The initial concept note discussed much larger annual savings from 150–250 kW of recovered heat. That is not supported by the wash/dry duty actually required for this plant. In the base case, wash and dry together need only about 159 MWhth/yr. If the wash line ran in a single 8- hour daily shift, that equates to roughly 72.7 kWth average thermal demand during the shift. That is useful, but it is far below a continuously usable 150–250 kW recovery case. This changes design decisions immediately: • A modest heat-recovery loop is justified. • A small hot-water buffer is justified to decouple the kiln from wash scheduling. • A very large thermal store is not justified unless a second heat customer exists on site. • Projected savings must be capped by actual heat consumption, not by theoretical recoverable exhaust heat. A 20 m³ hot-water buffer at a 35°C working temperature spread stores about 0.81 MWhth and is adequate to shift more than one operating day of wash/dry demand. A 70 m³ store would be materially oversized unless another process or neighboring plant bought the heat.
15 Figure 6. Energy, water and resilience schematic used for the base concept. Figure 7. Base-case electricity balance between on-site renewables and grid import.

16 8. Water, desalination and seawater cooling Gross wash-loop circulation is modeled at about 1,381 m³/yr, but with 82% recycle the fresh make-up requirement is only about 248 m³/yr. At current industrial-water tariffs this is a minor annual cost item rather than a capex driver. Table 5. Base-case water balance. Metric Value Unit Comment Gross wash circulation 1,380.51 m3/yr Total water put through wash loop before recycle Make-up water from utility network 248.49 m3/yr Fresh water needed after 82% recycle Recycle within wash loop 1,132.02 m3/yr Recovered via settling / filter press / recirculation tank Approx. blowdown / sludge bleed 248.49 m3/yr Assumed equal to make-up at steady state Useful low-grade heat needed by wash + dry 159.11 MWhth/yr Thermal sink that recovered kiln heat can realistically serve This leads to a strong design conclusion: a dedicated SWRO desalination plant should not be part of phase 1 unless industrial water is unavailable or extremely unreliable. The process simply does not consume enough fresh water for a stand-alone desalination system to earn its keep. The same logic applies to seawater cooling. It may become attractive later if the broader industrial parcel develops shared utility infrastructure, but it is not required by the base foam-glass process case. Including it too early only dilutes capital efficiency. The correct phase-1 water strategy is utility water connection, recirculation, sludge handling, and right- sized buffer tankage. Only after actual plant operation is understood should optional SWRO or seawater loops be revisited as part of a broader site-wide utility strategy.

17 9. Electrical resilience, battery role and diesel backup The electrical system should be designed as an industrial-quality micro-system embedded in the wider grid rather than as a standalone islanded plant. The main reasons are kiln continuity, harmonic management, and fast response to grid disturbances. The 1 MW / 2 MWh battery gives roughly 3.6 h of autonomy against the kiln's modeled running average load, and about 6.7 h of autonomy against a 300 kW hot-hold essential-load case. That makes it valuable for ride-through, controlled load reduction and black-start support while the diesel generator starts or the grid recovers. The battery should therefore be justified on four grounds: • ride-through during brief grid events; • fast load shaping and possible participation in system balancing; • smoother self-consumption of PV generation; • support for a controlled rather than chaotic response to outages. What the battery should not be sold as is a classic time-of-use arbitrage machine. The tariff spread between industrial high and low periods is too small to justify that story on its own. Table 6. Storage and resilience checks. Metric Value Unit Comment Battery energy 2.00 MWh Installed BESS energy Battery power 1.00 MW Installed BESS inverter power Battery autonomy at average annual plant load 4.32 hours If the full plant kept running at annual average load Battery autonomy at kiln running average load 3.64 hours If BESS carried only the running kiln average load Battery autonomy at 300 kW hot-hold essential load 6.67 hours Useful ride-through before diesel or grid returns 20 m3 hot-water storage at 35C delta 0.81 MWhth Enough for ~1.4 operating days of wash/dry thermal demand 70 m3 hot-water storage at 35C delta 2.85 MWhth Likely oversized unless there is another heat off-taker

18 10. Site, buildings and brownfield reality Using a former refinery parcel is strategically attractive. It offers industrial zoning logic, likely heavy-utility corridors, truck access and marine interface potential. But brownfields are never 'free'. They shift cost from greenfield civils into diligence, environmental management and uncertainty. The reference site plan assumes a planning area of roughly four hectares. That allows a process hall, receiving yard, warehouse/dispatch zone, utility yard, PV area, truck circulation and a small future expansion strip without forcing an overly tight layout. The real pre-FID gating item is not land size but site condition. Environmental baseline, geotechnical checks, drainage routing, stormwater handling, and existing buried services can all materially change civils cost. For that reason, the capex model carries dedicated brownfield survey / permitting cost and a meaningful contingency. • Do not commit to a specific plot before a desk environmental review and at least preliminary intrusive surveys. • Preserve one-way truck circulation and product dispatch space from the beginning; do not let energy assets consume the best logistics zones. • Treat corrosion and salt exposure as design-basis issues, not afterthoughts.

19 11. Staffing and operating model The staffing plan is deliberately light but not 'indie'. It assumes basic industrial discipline, limited robotics and a process that still needs human supervision and maintenance. The core plant plan excludes a large self-owned route-collection organization, which can remain outsourced or partnered. Table 7. Indicative core staffing plan. Role FTE Monthly gross USD Loaded annual USD Plant manager 1 6500 92,040.00 Production/process engineer 1 4800 67,968.00 Shift supervisors 3 3200 135,936.00 Kiln operators 6 2100 178,416.00 Sorting/wash/mill operators 5 1800 127,440.00 Packing/finishing operators 4 1700 96,288.00 Forklift/loader operators 3 1850 78,588.00 Maintenance mechanics 2 2500 70,800.00 Maintenance electrical/automation 1 3000 42,480.00 QC/lab technician 1 2200 31,152.00 Warehouse/logistics coordinator 1 2200 31,152.00 Procurement/admin/finance 2 2600 73,632.00 The core staffing plan totals 30 FTE and roughly 1,025,892 USD/yr of loaded payroll. That is materially higher than a hand-wavy low-headcount concept, but it is much more defendable for a 24/7 thermal process on an island. Shift structure should place the kiln and quality-critical functions on continuous coverage, while washing, some finishing activities and parts of dispatch can run with more limited shifts if inventory buffers are maintained.

20 12. CAPEX estimate and technology procurement Core CAPEX is currently estimated at about 19,603,000 USD excluding optional SWRO and seawater systems. Optional resilience add-ons in the current line-item view are another 480,000 USD, but these are explicitly not recommended for phase 1. The single biggest cost mistake at concept stage would be to look only at a kiln vendor's ex-works list price and mistake that for a real installed project cost. On an island brownfield, the final capital number is driven by buildings, civils, installation, electrical integration, controls, contingency and logistics almost as much as by the thermal core equipment itself. 22 Figure 8. CAPEX by category. Long-lead procurement should focus early on the kiln, optical sorting system, fine mill/classifier package and control architecture. These packages drive both lead time and process performance. Vendor RFQs should be issued before full civil commitment so that the basis of design remains aligned with real equipment footprints and services.

23 13. OPEX and base economics In the integrated base operating case, including the ancillary-product branch, total modeled revenue is about 4,184,169 USD/yr and total OPEX about 2,795,588 USD/yr, producing EBITDA of about 1,388,582 USD/yr or 33.2%. This is a workable but not invincible business case. The ancillary branch improves the headline numbers and should be included in the official model, but it does not remove the project’s dependence on local price realization and on keeping the factory fed. The conservative case remains much weaker, which means the project should only proceed after the commercial and feedstock gates are genuinely closed. Table 9. Revenue and OPEX bridge by scenario. 24 Figure 9. Base-case integrated OPEX breakdown including ancillary direct cost. The financial model should be interpreted as a concept-level decision aid, not as financing-grade certainty. Its job is to tell management where reality matters most. In this project, the most important sensitivities are product selling price, feedstock capture, and hidden brownfield cost. Water and desalination barely matter. Oversized heat-recovery hardware does not help. Tariff arbitrage does not save the battery case. A simple 10-year unlevered model is included in the Excel workbook. Under the current base assumptions, a concept-level simple payback on core CAPEX remains relatively long, which is exactly why product- market validation and CAPEX tightening are mandatory before FID.
